'''David George Campbell''' (born January 28, 1949, in [[Decatur, Illinois]], United States) is an American educator, ecologist, environmentalist, and award-winning author of non-fiction. He is the son of George R. Campbell (1918–2004) and Jean Blossom Weilepp (1917–1998). 
 
Campbell spent his childhood on [[Eleuthera Island]], Bahamas, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and Grosse Pointe, Michigan. He received a BS in biology from [[Kalamazoo College]] (1971), an MS in biology from the [[University of Michigan]] (1973), and a Ph.D. from the [[Johns Hopkins School of Public Health]] (1984). He is married to Karen S. Lowell, a [[phytochemist]]; they have a daughter.

==Bahama Islands==
From 1974-1977, Campbell was the executive Director of the [[Bahamas National Trust]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bnt.bs/ |title=The Bahamas National Trust - Home |publisher=Bnt.bs |date= |accessdate=2012-06-18}}</ref> the organization responsible for parks, reserves, and setting priorities for wildlife conservation in the [[The Bahamas|Bahamian Archipelago]]. As director he established priorities for the protection of island-endemic species including the [[Northern Bahamian rock iguana|rock iguanas]] (''[[Cyclura]]'' spp.) and [[hutias]],<ref>Campbell, D. G., K. S. Lowell & M. E. Lightbourn. 1991. The effect of introduced hutias (''Geocapromys ingrahami'') on the woody vegetation of Little Wax Cay, Bahamas.</ref> and started the process of the Bahamas becoming a signatory to the Convention on Trade in Endangered Species ([[CITES]]). His career in the Bahamas culminated in the publication of ''The Ephemeral Islands'', the first natural history of the archipelago to be published since the 1800s.

==Chincoteague Bay==
From 1978-1983, Campbell elucidated the etiology of gray crab disease, an [[Amoeba|amoebic]] [[pathogen]] that every spring kills ca. 30% of the blue crabs (''[[Callinectes sapidus]]'') in [[Chincoteague Bay]], VA. His research showed that the disease is spread by cannibalism, mediated by ambient temperature and salinity.<ref>Campbell, D. G. 1984. The Abundance and Distribution of ''Paramoeba perniciosa''. Ph.D. Dissertation. The Johns Hopkins University. 188 pages</ref>

==Amazonia==
In 1974, Campbell was a botanical explorer at the Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da Amazônia ([[INPA]])<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.inpa.gov.br/ |title=Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da Amazônia |publisher=INPA |date= |accessdate=2012-06-18}}</ref> in Manaus, Brazil, from where he staged expeditions to study the ethnobotany of the Jamamaji and [[Paumari]] Native Americans.<ref>Prance, G. T., D. G. Campbell & B. W Nelson. 1977. The ethnobotany of the Paumari Indians (Rio Purus), ''[[Economic Botany]]''. 31. 129-139</ref> Campbell joined the scientific staff of the [[New York Botanical Garden]] from 1984 to 1990, conducting floristic inventories throughout the Brazilian [[Amazon basin]] as part of the Projeto Flora Amazônica program;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.biodiversidadeamazonica.net/flora/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=44&Itemid=53 |title=Flora amazonica |accessdate=2010-08-15 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110910154224/http://www.biodiversidadeamazonica.net/flora/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=44&Itemid=53 |archivedate=2011-09-10 }}</ref> destinations included O Deserto on the [[Rio Xingu]] ([[Pará]]),<ref>Campbell, D. G., D. C. Daly, G. T. Prance & U. N. Maciel. 1986. Quantitative ecological inventory of terra firme and [[Freshwater swamp forest|várzea]] tropical forest on the Rio Xingu, Brazilian Amazon. ''[[Brittonia]]'' 38(4): 369-393</ref> the [[Rio Falsino]] ([[Amapá]]), {{Interlanguage link multi|Reserva Biológica Ilha de Maracá|pt}} ([[Roraima]]),  the [[Môa River|Rio Moa]] and [[Serra do Divisor National Park]] ([[Acre (state)|Acre]]).

These expeditions resulted in several notable papers on [[allelopathy]],<ref>Campbell, D. G., P. M. Richardson & A. R. Rosas. 1989. Field screening for allelopathy in tropical forest trees, particularly ''Duroia hirsuta'', in the Brazilian Amazon. ''[[Biochemical Systematics & Ecology]]''. 17(5): 403-407</ref> [[várzea floodplain forests]]<ref>Campbell, D. G. J. L. Stone & A. Rosas, Jr. 1992. A comparison of the phytosociology of three floodplain (várzea) forests of known ages, Rio Juruá, western Brazilian Amazon. ''[[Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society]]'' 108: 213-237.</ref><ref>Campbell, D. G. 1994. Scale and patterns of community structure in Amazonian forests. Pages 181-199 In: P. Edwards and R. May (eds.) ''Large-Scale Ecology and Conservation Biology''. Blackwell. Oxford.</ref> and anthropogenic [[lianaceous]] forests.<ref>Balée, W. & D. G. Campbell. 1990. Ecological aspects of liana forest, [[Xingu River]], Amazonian Brazil. ''[[Biotropica]]''. 22(1): 36-47.</ref> The Acre expeditions were chronicled in ''A Land of Ghosts'', which won the [[Lannan Literary Award for Nonfiction]].

==Antarctica, Africa and Asia==
In the late 1980s and 1990s, Campbell shifted his research. He examined the impacts of elephants on west African forests,<ref>Campbell, D. G. 1989. Gap formation in tropical forest canopy by [[elephants]], Oveng, Gabon, Central Africa. ''Biotropica''. 23(2): 195-196</ref> the diversity of subtropical forests in southern China,<ref>Z Wang, S. An, D. G. Campbell, X. Yang & X. Zhu Xuelei. 1999, Biodiversity of the montane rainforest in Diaoluo Mountain, [[Hainan]]. ''[[Acta Ecologica Sinica]]''. 19(1): 61-67.</ref> conducted research on the pathologies of [[krill]] and marine [[isopods]] in the waters of [[Admiralty Bay (South Shetland Islands)|Admiralty Bay]], [[King George Island (Antarctica)|King George Island]] (one of the South Shetlands of the Antarctic Peninsula), joined the sixth Brazilian expedition to [[Antarctica]] (1988), and lived at that nation's [[Comandante Ferraz Base]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.furg.br/esantar/ferraz.htm |accessdate=August 15, 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090225123345/http://www2.furg.br/esantar/ferraz.htm |archivedate=February 25, 2009 |title=Estação de Apoio Antártico - Sobre a Esantar }}</ref> This experience was chronicled in ''The Crystal Desert'', which won the [[Burroughs Medal]], the PEN Martha Albrand Award and the Houghton Mifflin Literary Fellowship Award.

==Grinnell College==
Since 1991 Campbell has been a professor of biology, chair of environmental studies and Henry R. Luce Professor <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hluce.org/hrluceprofship.aspx |title=Henry R. Luce Professorships |publisher=Hluce.org |date= |accessdate=2012-06-18 |archive-date=2012-09-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903235904/http://www.hluce.org/hrluceprofship.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref> in Nations and the Global Environment at [[Grinnell College]].<ref>{{cite web|title=David Campbell, Henry L. Professor of Nations and the Global Environment|website=Grinnell College|url=https://www.grinnell.edu/users/campbell}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.grinnell.edu/academic/biology/faculty/dcampbell-books |title=Books by David G. Campbell - Biology &#124; Grinnell College |publisher=Grinnell.edu |date=2012-04-15 |accessdate=2012-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303161335/http://www.grinnell.edu/academic/biology/faculty/dcampbell-books |archive-date=2012-03-03 |url-status=dead }}</ref> From 1994 to 2007 he and his Grinnell students conducted studies on the historical ecology of the Yucatec, Mopan and Kekchi [[Maya peoples|Maya]] of Belize, using quantitative methods to test the long-held hypothesis that the Maya Forest is [[Human impact on the environment|anthropogenic]],<ref>Campbell, D. G., A. Ford, K. S. Lowell, J. Walker, J. K. Lake, C. Ocampo-Raeder, A. Townesmith & M. J. Balick. 2006. The feral forests of the eastern Petén. Pages 21-55 In: W. Balée & C. Erickson (eds.). ''Time and Complexity in Historical Ecology - Studies in the Neotropical Lowlands''. Columbia University Press. NY. {{ISBN|0-231-50961-8}}</ref> even suggesting that its species composition was due to post-contact ranching.<ref>Campbell, D. G., J. Guittar, K. S. Lowell. 2008. Are Colonial Pastures The Ancestors of The Contemporary Maya Forest? ''J. Ethnobiology'' 28(2):278–289 {{doi|10.2993/0278-0771-28.2.278}}</ref> In 2010 Campbell extrapolated this controversial hypothesis to Amazonia, presenting evidence that pre-Columbian Native Americans caused a large-scale extinction of botanical diversity before the Europeans arrived.<ref>Campbell, D. G. Botanical extinction in Amazonia: was there a Neotropical “Langsamenkrieg”? Pages 173–188 In. E. Barrone-Visigalli & A. Roosevelt (eds.) ''Amaz'hommes, Sciences de l’Homme et Sciences de la Nature en Amazonie?'' {{Interlanguage link multi|IBIS Rouge Éditions|fr}}, Matoury. {{ISBN|978-2-84450-372-5}}</ref>
